projects.title: Wager365 - Mobile App
projects.tagline: Live sports odds and a multi-currency wallet, designed and built end-to-end.
projects.about: Wager365 is a sports betting app bringing live football, basketball and tennis odds into one board, with a bet slip that supports parlays and a wallet that takes bank transfer, card or crypto deposits, settling in whatever currency the user sets for their account. I designed the full product from onboarding through settlement, then built it as a working React Native app with a Firebase backend, including a tested settlement engine and a staged migration path for moving money logic server-side.

gallery.alt: Wager365 home screen on a phone in hand

columns.heading: The Problem
columns.body:
Traditional betting platforms can often feel cluttered and overwhelming.

Users may need to navigate through:

- Large numbers of betting markets

- Complicated odds

- Depositing with crypto

- Difficult-to-understand bet slips

- Fragmented transaction experiences

For a crypto-powered platform, these problems become even more important because users need to understand **both their bets and their money**.

columns.heading: Design Goals
columns.body:
The product experience was designed around five key goals:

**Clarity**
Make odds, markets, balances, and potential winnings easy to understand.

**Speed**
Reduce the number of steps required to discover a match and place a wager.

**Deposit**
Make deposits easy across cryptocurrencies, stablecoins and fiat currency.

**Trust**
Create an interface that feels reliable enough for users to confidently manage funds and bets.

**Simplicity**
Hide unnecessary complexity without limiting functionality for experienced users.

columns.heading: Design Decisions
columns.body:
**Why fintech-inspired UI?**

Money-related products require a strong sense of clarity and trust. Wager365 therefore borrows interaction patterns from fintech products rather than relying entirely on traditional sportsbook conventions.

**Why a simplified bet slip?**

The bet slip is where a user's selections become an actual wager. Reducing unnecessary information and emphasizing the stake and potential return makes the final decision easier to understand.

**Why strong information hierarchy?**

Sports betting interfaces contain a huge amount of numerical information. Typography, spacing, grouping, and contrast were therefore used to create a clear hierarchy between matches, markets, odds, and secondary information.

columns.heading: Outcome
columns.body:
Wager365 demonstrates how a complex sports betting product can be approached through the lens of **product design, fintech UX, and Web3**.

The project allowed me to explore:

- Sports betting UX

- Financial product interfaces

- Crypto wallet experiences

- Information-heavy dashboards

- Responsive product design

- Complex interaction flows

- Design systems and visual hierarchy

More importantly, the project challenged me to design for a product where **speed, clarity, and trust directly influence the user's experience.**

gallery.alt: Wager365 create account and log in screens
Wager365 search, live games, bet slip and match detail screens
Wager365 won, lost, deposit method and notification screens

columns.heading: Final Statement
columns.body: Wager365 was an exploration of what a modern crypto-powered sportsbook could look and feel like combining the speed of digital assets with the familiarity of a well-designed sports betting platform.

projects.title: Scribe - Web App
projects.tagline: A modern doc editor for writing, organizing, and managing your ideas.
projects.about: Scribe is a cross-platform document editor and workspace designed to bring writing, organization, and collaboration into one focused environment. I designed the product experience from the ground up, exploring the desktop workspace, document editor, navigation, onboarding, authentication, and supporting product ecosystem. The experience is designed desktop-first, with a flexible foundation that can extend naturally to mobile and other platforms.

gallery.alt: Scribe document editor with Ask Scribe AI on selected text

columns.heading: The Problem
columns.body:
When I was working on my final-year project at university, I struggled to find a document editor that made writing and researching easier. Most of the tools I tried either lacked useful AI features or placed them behind expensive plans.

But AI wasn’t the only problem.

My group also struggled to work together. We edited documents separately, shared different versions, and sent files back and forth on WhatsApp just to review and make corrections. It became difficult to keep track of changes, feedback, and the latest version of the document.

That experience made me realize there was an opportunity to build something better — **a workspace where writing, AI, document management, and collaboration could happen in one place.**

That idea became **Scribe**.

columns.heading: Who It’s For
columns.body:
Scribe is built for people who write, organize, and work with documents regularly.

- **Students** — for assignments, research, notes, and group projects.

- **Researchers** — for writing, organizing research, and refining ideas with AI.

- **Writers & Creators** — for drafting, editing, and developing ideas in one workspace.

- **Teams** — for working together on documents, leaving feedback, and making changes in real time.

- **Professionals** — for reports, proposals, meeting notes, and everyday documentation.

**One workspace for writing, thinking, and working together.**

columns.heading: Design Decisions
columns.body:
**1. Real-time collaboration vs. traditional file sharing**
I considered keeping Scribe focused on individual document editing and using file sharing for collaboration. I rejected this because my own experience showed how difficult it is to manage multiple versions. Instead, Scribe allows users to work on the same document, leave comments, and review changes together.

**2. AI as a separate feature vs. part of the writing experience**
I considered making AI a standalone tool within Scribe. I chose to integrate it directly into the document experience so users can refine, summarize, and reorganize content without leaving their workflow.

**3. Simple workspace vs. feature-heavy dashboard**
I considered adding more tools and navigation options upfront. I rejected this in favor of a simpler workspace that keeps the document at the center and makes the core actions easy to access.

columns.heading: Workspaces
columns.body:
Documents can quickly become difficult to manage when school work, personal projects, research, and professional work all live in the same place. Scribe organizes documents into dedicated workspaces such as **Personal, Projects, Work, and Research**, giving each area its own space while keeping everything accessible from one place.

For shared workspaces, admins can invite team members, add and organize documents, and control who has access to different content. This makes it easier for teams to collaborate without losing control of their workspace or document permissions.

Each file also provides clear information about its latest activity, including **when it was last saved and who made the change**. This gives users a quick way to understand the current state of a document and makes it easier to identify the latest version when multiple people are working together.

columns.heading: Contextual AI
columns.body:
The goal was to make AI feel like part of the writing process rather than a separate tool users had to switch to.

I explored how common writing tasks such as **rewriting, shortening, expanding, correcting, and changing tone** could happen directly within the document. This led to contextual AI actions appearing alongside the selected text, keeping the user focused on their work.

The key design decision was to make AI **available at the moment it is useful**, rather than requiring users to open a separate AI interface and explain what they want.

columns.heading: Document-level AI
columns.body:
I wanted Scribe AI to go beyond editing individual sentences and help users **understand and work with entire documents**.

I mapped common document-level tasks such as **summarizing content, finding key information, extracting important points, and understanding long documents**. These became part of the broader Document AI experience.

The main design principle was to keep these capabilities connected to the document itself, so users can move from **reading → understanding → acting** without leaving their workspace.

columns.heading: Version History
columns.body:
Never lose track of your latest version

While working on documents with others, it’s easy to lose track of what changed, who changed it, or which version is the right one.

Scribe keeps every change in one timeline. Users can see who made changes and when, preview earlier versions, compare changes, and restore a previous version when needed.

**The flow**

Open history → Preview or compare → Restore

Restoring never overwrites the current document. Instead, Scribe creates a new version, keeping the existing history safe and accessible.

columns.heading: Comments & Collaboration
columns.body:
Working with other people on the same document can quickly become difficult when edits, feedback, and conversations happen across different tools. Team members may have to send files back and forth, explain which section needs changes, or search through messages to find previous feedback.

Scribe brings the entire collaboration process into the document. Users can work on the same document in real time, see who else is editing, highlight specific sections, leave comments, reply to feedback, and keep conversations attached to the work they relate to.

The goal was to make collaboration feel like a natural part of writing rather than a separate workflow. Instead of switching between the document, messaging apps, and email, users can write, review, discuss, and make changes together in one place.

columns.heading: Integrations
columns.body:
Most people already have years of documents stored across different tools and services. Asking them to move everything into a new workspace would only create more friction and make the transition harder. Instead, Scribe is designed to work alongside the tools people already use.

Scribe connects with **Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive**, allowing users to bring their existing files into their workspace without having to constantly switch between different platforms. Files can be opened, accessed, and kept connected while users continue working from within Scribe.

The goal was to make integrations feel simple rather than technical. Each service can be connected or disconnected with a single action from Settings, giving users control over which services they want to use and keeping their existing workflow intact.

columns.heading: Onboarding
columns.body:
Onboarding has one clear goal: **get users from sign-up to creating their first document with as little friction as possible.** After creating an account and verifying their email, users choose the type of workspace they want, give it a name, and decide how they want to get started. They can import existing files such as **PDF, DOCX, and XLSX**, or start with a blank workspace and create something new.

A simple progress indicator keeps users aware of where they are in the setup process and how many steps remain. Each step is focused on one decision, keeping the experience clear and easy to move through without overwhelming users with unnecessary setup.

columns.heading: Settings
columns.body: Settings are grouped by what people actually look for: preferences (General, Appearance, Notifications, Keyboard shortcuts), account, workspaces and data. Storage shows usage broken down by PDFs, documents and spreadsheets, so users can see what's taking up space before they hit their limit.

columns.heading: How I Know It Works
columns.body:
I tested the early Scribe experience with **5 classmates from my final-year project group**, the same kind of users I was designing for. During the test, they found it difficult to understand where to access shared documents and how to leave feedback on specific sections.

Based on this, I made **collaboration and comments more visible within the document workspace**, allowing users to work on the same document, comment directly on content, and reply within a thread.

One key finding was that users understood the document editor immediately, but needed clearer visual cues to discover the collaboration features.

projects.title: EchoYou
projects.tagline: An AI-powered communication assistant designed to help people take control of their inbox.
projects.about:
Email is still one of the most important communication tools for modern professionals, but managing an inbox can quickly become overwhelming.

EchoYou is an AI-powered productivity platform designed to help users understand, organize, and act on their emails without constantly working through their inbox manually.

The product combines email management, AI assistance, calendar intelligence, and automated actions into one experience.

gallery.alt: EchoYou inbox and AI assistant on a laptop

columns.heading: The Problem
columns.body:
The modern inbox is more than a place for receiving messages.

It's where people manage:

- Work conversations

- Meetings

- Tasks

- Documents

- Follow-ups

- Notifications

- Personal communication

- Important deadlines

As the number of emails increases, users spend more time **sorting and processing information** instead of actually acting on it.

columns.heading: The Opportunity
columns.body:
Most email tools focus primarily on helping users **write or organize emails**.

EchoYou explores a broader approach.

Instead of being another email client, it acts as an **intelligent layer on top of communication**.

It can help users:

**Understand → Prioritize → Respond → Schedule → Act**

This makes email management feel less like administrative work and more like having a personal communication assistant.

columns.heading: Design Goals
columns.body:
**01. Reduce inbox overload**

Help users quickly understand what deserves their attention.

**02. Turn emails into actions**

Identify tasks, meetings, follow-ups, and important information inside conversations.

**03. Save time**

Automate repetitive communication tasks where appropriate.

**04. Keep users in control**

AI should assist the user rather than silently making important decisions on their behalf.

columns.heading: Understanding the User
columns.body:
EchoYou is designed for people who deal with high volumes of communication.

**The Professional**

Receives dozens of emails every day and needs to quickly identify what requires attention.

**The Founder / Manager**

Manages conversations, meetings, clients, and follow-ups across multiple projects.

**The Freelancer**

Uses email for client communication, proposals, scheduling, and project coordination.

Across these users, the problem is similar:

**“I don't want to spend my day managing my inbox.”**

columns.heading: Product Experience
columns.body:
EchoYou brings several workflows together:

**Inbox Intelligence**

AI categorizes and prioritizes incoming emails.

**Email Summaries**

Long conversations are condensed into useful summaries.

**Smart Replies**

AI generates contextual responses that users can review and edit.

**Action Extraction**

Important tasks, deadlines, and requests can be identified from emails.

**Calendar Intelligence**

EchoYou detects scheduling-related conversations and connects them with the user's calendar.

**Agent Mode**

Users can give EchoYou permission to perform specific low-risk actions on their behalf.

columns.heading: Inbox Experience
columns.body:
The inbox was designed around **priority rather than chronology alone**.

Instead of presenting every email with equal visual weight, EchoYou can help surface the conversations that require attention.

For each conversation, users can quickly understand:

**Who sent it → What it's about → Why it matters → What action is required**

AI-generated summaries reduce the need to open every message just to understand its context.

columns.heading: AI Email Summaries
columns.body:
Long email threads can contain dozens of messages and multiple topics.

EchoYou condenses these conversations into concise summaries.

For example:

**Project Update — Client

Summary**

The client approved the latest design direction and requested the final assets by Friday.

**Action required**

Send final assets before Friday.

This transforms a long conversation into something the user can understand in seconds.

columns.heading: Smart Replies
columns.body:
EchoYou can generate contextual responses based on the conversation.

Instead of producing generic AI-generated text, the experience is designed around the actual context of the email.

Users can:

- Generate a response

- Adjust the tone

- Shorten the response

- Expand the response

- Edit manually

- Review before sending

The user remains the final decision-maker.

columns.heading: Turning Emails Into Tasks
columns.body:
One of the core ideas behind EchoYou is that **emails often contain hidden tasks**.

For example:

“Could you send the revised proposal before Thursday?”

EchoYou can identify:

**Task:** Send revised proposal
**Deadline:** Thursday

The user can then add it to their task workflow instead of relying on memory.

This connects communication with execution.

columns.heading: Calendar Intelligence
columns.body:
Scheduling conversations often involve multiple back-and-forth emails.

EchoYou can identify scheduling intent and surface useful information.

For example:

“Are you available for a meeting next Tuesday?”

Instead of manually opening a calendar and checking availability, EchoYou can surface relevant available times.

Users can review the suggested schedule before confirming.

columns.heading: Agent Mode
columns.body:
Agent Mode extends EchoYou beyond suggestions.

Users can define what EchoYou is allowed to do automatically.

For example:

**Allowed**

- Categorize newsletters

- Archive promotional emails

- Draft routine replies

- Identify follow-up tasks

**Requires Approval**

- Send an important email

- Schedule a meeting

- Reply to a client

- Modify an existing calendar event

The design makes permissions explicit so users understand **what the AI can and cannot do.**

columns.heading: AI Assistant
columns.body:
EchoYou also provides a conversational interface for interacting with the inbox.

Users can ask:

**“What do I need to respond to today?”

“Summarize my conversation with John.”

“Which emails are waiting for my response?”

“What meetings were mentioned in my emails this week?”**

The assistant becomes a natural interface for navigating large amounts of communication.

columns.heading: Key Design Decisions
columns.body:
**AI should explain, not just act**

Users should understand what the AI has identified or intends to do.

**Human approval for important actions**

Actions involving external communication or important calendar changes can require user confirmation.

**Progressive automation**

Users can start with AI suggestions and gradually give EchoYou more permissions as they become comfortable.

**Context over commands**

Rather than forcing users to learn complicated AI prompts, EchoYou surfaces relevant actions directly within their workflow.

columns.heading: Reflection
columns.body:
Designing EchoYou pushed me to think beyond the traditional email interface.

The key question throughout the project was:

**What if your inbox could understand what needs to happen next?**

That led to an experience where emails aren't treated as isolated messages, but as potential **tasks, conversations, meetings, and actions**.

The design ultimately explores a future where AI handles the repetitive parts of communication while users remain in control of the decisions that matter.

projects.title: Orbit - Mobile App
projects.tagline: Orbit is a multi-currency fintech app that allows users to send, receive, and hold Naira, USD, Euro, and stablecoins seamlessly in one place.
projects.about:
Orbit is a modern multi-currency finance app built for a borderless world.
We help people send, receive, convert, and manage money seamlessly across Naira, USD, Euro, and stablecoins all from one secure platform.

Designed for freelancers, global professionals, travelers, and digital-first users, Orbit combines the simplicity of modern banking with the flexibility of digital assets. Whether you’re paying internationally, saving in stable currencies, or transferring funds instantly, Orbit keeps your money moving without limits.

gallery.alt: Orbit home screen on a phone in hand

columns.heading: The Problem
columns.body:
The modern financial ecosystem is fragmented.

Users managing money across borders often have to move between:

- Traditional bank accounts

- Crypto wallets

- Currency exchange platforms

- Payment apps

- Stablecoin wallets

- International transfer services

Each platform introduces its own interface, terminology, and transaction flow.

This creates unnecessary friction, especially for users who simply want to **hold, move, exchange, and spend their money.**

columns.heading: The Opportunity
columns.body:
Stablecoins create an interesting bridge between traditional finance and digital assets.

But the underlying technology can be complicated.

Users shouldn't need to understand:

- Blockchain networks

- Gas fees

- Wallet infrastructure

- Token standards

- On-chain transactions

just to move money.

The opportunity was to abstract that complexity behind a familiar financial experience.

gallery.alt: Orbit create account and log in screens

columns.heading: Design Goals
columns.body:
**01. Simplify**

Reduce the complexity of managing multiple currencies and financial accounts.

**02. Connect**

Bring fiat and stablecoins together within one wallet experience.

**03. Build Trust**

Make balances, transactions, rates, and financial actions clear.

**04. Enable Movement**

Make sending money across currencies feel as easy as sending a local transfer.

columns.heading: Product Experience
columns.body:
Orbit revolves around four core experiences:

**Multi-Currency Wallet**

Users can manage their ₦, $, €, USDT, and USDC balances from one place.

**Global Transfers**

Users can send money to other people without needing to understand the underlying financial infrastructure.

**Currency Conversion**

Users can move between supported currencies while clearly seeing the amount, rate, and fees before confirming.

**Financial Insights**

Orbit provides users with a clearer picture of how they're using and moving their money.

gallery.alt: Orbit send money: recipient, country and bank account details
Orbit transfer details, PIN, success and transaction details screens
Orbit transfer to an Orbit user, from recipient to transaction details
Orbit crypto transfer: network, address, details and confirmation
Orbit crypto transfer success and transaction details

columns.heading: Final Outcome
columns.body:
Orbit explores what a financial platform could look like when **traditional money and digital assets are treated as parts of the same ecosystem.**

The project allowed me to explore:

- Fintech product design

- Stablecoin experiences

- Multi-currency wallets

- Payment infrastructure

- Financial dashboards

- Transaction UX

- Web3 abstraction

- Responsive product design

- Design systems

Ultimately, Orbit isn't about making crypto more complicated. It's about making the complexity **disappear.**

projects.title: Coin Compass - Mobile App
projects.tagline: Your smart financial guide, built to help you navigate money management with confidence.
projects.about:
CoinCompass is your smart financial guide, built to help you navigate money management with confidence. Designed for the modern user, CoinCompass combines intelligent insights, intuitive tools, and real-time tracking to help you make smarter decisions about your finances.
Whether you're budgeting, investing, or just trying to stay on top of your spending, CoinCompass empowers you to take control with ease. Our sleek interface, personalized recommendations, and seamless experience make managing money less stressful—and a lot more rewarding.

gallery.alt: Coin Compass home, insights and profile screens

columns.heading: The Problem
columns.body:
Managing personal finances can quickly become complicated.

People often have their money spread across different accounts, while financial information is presented as disconnected numbers.

Users may struggle with:

- Understanding where their money goes

- Tracking spending

- Setting realistic financial goals

- Knowing how much they can afford to spend

- Planning for future expenses

- Understanding their overall financial position

The challenge wasn't simply to create another budgeting app. It was to help people understand what their money is doing, and what to do next.

columns.heading: The Opportunity
columns.body:
CoinCompass explores the idea of combining **personal finance management with intelligent financial guidance**.

Instead of simply showing:

**Income → Expenses → Balance**

the product helps users understand the relationship between those numbers.

For example:

**You're spending more on dining this month.

Your savings goal is 68% complete.

You have ₦45,000 available after your upcoming expenses.**

This turns financial data into something users can actually understand and act on.

images.alt: Sign up and sign in screens

columns.heading: Design Goals
columns.body:
**01. Make finance understandable**

Present financial information in a way that feels simple and approachable.

**02. Give users context**

Don't just show numbers. Help users understand what those numbers mean.

**03. Encourage better financial habits**

Help users stay aware of their spending, savings, and goals.

**04. Personalize the experience**

Use intelligent insights to make the product feel relevant to each user's financial situation.

gallery.alt: Coin Compass send and request money screens

columns.heading: The Product Experience
columns.body:
CoinCompass is centered around four major experiences:

**Financial Overview**

A single place to understand the user's current financial position.

**Spending**

Track transactions and understand spending patterns.

**Goals**

Create and monitor financial goals.

**AI Financial Advisor**

Ask questions and receive personalized financial insights.

The experience is designed around a simple cycle:

**Understand → Plan → Act → Improve**

columns.heading: AI Financial Advisor
columns.body:
The AI advisor is one of the key parts of CoinCompass.

Instead of navigating through financial dashboards to find answers, users can interact with their finances conversationally.

For example:

**“How much did I spend this month?”

“Where am I spending the most?”

“How much should I save each month for my goal?”

“Can I afford this purchase based on my current spending?”**

The AI layer makes financial information more accessible by allowing users to interact with it naturally.

gallery.alt: Coin Compass request and add funds screens
Coin Compass CashBuddy AI advisor and notification screens

columns.heading: Key Design Decisions
columns.body:
**Information hierarchy over information density**

Financial apps can easily become dashboards full of numbers.

CoinCompass prioritizes the information users need first and progressively reveals deeper details.

**Insights alongside data**

Instead of making users interpret every chart themselves, the product introduces contextual insights alongside financial information.

**Goals as a first-class experience**

Saving isn't treated as an afterthought. Goals are integrated directly into the user's financial overview.

**Conversational finance**

The AI advisor gives users another way to interact with their finances without requiring them to understand complicated financial terminology.

columns.heading: Outcome
columns.body:
CoinCompass became an exploration of how **AI can make personal finance more understandable and personalized.**

Rather than building a product that simply tells users how much money they have, the concept focuses on helping users understand:

**Where their money goes.

What they're working toward.

What their financial patterns look like.**

And ultimately:

**What they can do next.**
